correctness.rationale: The two moments fix the affine part uniquely for every L² input g=f'', and the squared joint norm is the top eigenvalue of the resulting evaluation Gram matrix. Independent exact integration, using the affine projection (1−u)²[x(1+2u)−u] of the hinge as a function of x, reproduced the full Gram polynomial and both centering differences. The trial at d=188/625 is below 41/100000. The diagonal barrier confines every competitive site to one of the two stated short intervals; the derivative-kernel bound excludes two sites in the same interval, including site collisions. In the resulting rectangle both Rayleigh bounds strictly improve on moving the midpoint to 1/2 at fixed gap. On the confined gap range the antisymmetric eigenvalue decreases, and the symmetric eigenvalue increases for d≥0.3008. The sign bracket gives precisely the stated active crossing: smaller d is excluded by the decreasing mode, larger d by the increasing one. This comparison with an attained candidate covers endpoints and does not assume compactness of the distinct-pair domain. At the crossing the Gram matrix is a positive scalar times the identity, giving exactly the stated two-dimensional span of norming second derivatives. Independent high-precision evaluation reproduced d=0.300804514991272228562… and the squared norm 0.000409822706363592947851… .
residual_risks: The numerical decimals are supplementary; the exact rational barriers and crossing proof establish globality. No proof-assistant verification is claimed.

value.rationale: The operator measures the worst total observation energy for a unit curvature-energy signal after affine detrending. It is natural to ask which two sites minimize that response. The answer classifies all free sites rather than merely optimizing a symmetric ansatz. The exact eigenvalue collision and corresponding norming modes reveal why the optimum is attained there and provide a sharp trace-design benchmark.
residual_risks: Value is for the particular sharp two-site forward norm, not a claim about optimal reconstruction, more sites or unequal weights.
